title: Talking It Over
theme: Discussion and communication: building on what others say
objectives: I can name what a speaker is doing in a discussion using ten precise verbs.
I can respond to a classmate's idea by acknowledging it, challenging it, or agreeing with it.
I can tell the difference between agreeing, reaching a consensus, and voting.
I can write a short discussion exchange that uses at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Sixth-grade standards ask students to take part in discussions that build on others' ideas, but many students lack the verbs that name what they are doing. This unit gives them ten: ways to put forward an idea (propose, assert, emphasize, reiterate), ways to react to someone else (respond, acknowledge, challenge, interject), and ways to come together (concur, consensus). Students practice choosing the verb that fits the move they want to make, which also strengthens how they read speeches, interviews, and debates.

words.def: To answer or react to what someone has said or done.
words.ex: Maya waited for her classmate to finish before she responded to the question.
words.ex2: The fire alarm sounded, and the students responded by walking quickly to the exits.
words.nonExample: Looking away and saying nothing is not responding.

apps.academic: In a discussion, respond to the previous speaker before you add a new idea.
apps.writing: Use respond with to: respond to a question, a letter, or an event.

cloze.s: When the teacher asked a question, three students raised their hands to ___.

cloze2.s: Emergency crews ___ within minutes of the call, with sirens blaring down the street.

misuse.s: She responded to the email by never writing back or sending any message at all.
misuse.why: To respond is to answer or react; sending no message is not a response.

visual.alt: A speech bubble with an arrow curving back to the speaker.

words.frame: When someone says ___, I respond by ___.

words.def: To accept that something is true, or to show that you have noticed someone.
words.ex: The coach acknowledged that the other team had played better.
words.ex2: Dana nodded to acknowledge the bus driver as she stepped off.
words.nonExample: Pretending you did not hear a question is not acknowledging it.
words.rel: showing you noticed or accept something

apps.academic: A strong argument acknowledges the other side before explaining why it disagrees.
apps.spoken: I want to acknowledge that you worked hard on this.
apps.writing: Use acknowledge to show that you accept a point, even if you will disagree next.

cloze.s: Before disagreeing, a good debater will ___ the strong points the other side has made.

cloze2.s: Everyone in the choir wanted the director to ___ their hard work with a few kind words.

misuse.s: He acknowledged her good idea by pretending that he had not heard it.
misuse.why: To acknowledge is to show you noticed or accept; pretending not to hear is the opposite.

visual.alt: A waving hand beside a pair of eyes.

words.def: To give special importance to something so that people notice it.
words.ex: The speaker emphasized the last point by pausing and raising her voice.
words.ex2: The poster emphasizes safety by printing the word in bright red letters.
words.nonExample: Mumbling a fact quickly does not emphasize it.

apps.academic: Authors emphasize an idea by repeating it or placing it at the end.
apps.spoken: I want to emphasize that this is really important.
apps.writing: Use emphasize with a thing that you want the reader to remember.

cloze.s: To ___ how serious the problem was, the principal showed photographs of the flooded gym.

cloze2.s: Underlining a key word in your notes can ___ it, so that it jumps out when you study.

misuse.s: He emphasized the danger by saying it was nothing to worry about.
misuse.why: To emphasize is to give importance; saying it is nothing to worry about downplays it.

visual.alt: An exclamation mark beside a megaphone.

words.frame: I want to emphasize that ___ because ___.

words.def: To question whether something is true or right and ask for proof.

senses.def: A difficult task that tests your skill or effort.
senses.example: Climbing the tall wall was a challenge, but Hana made it to the top.

words.ex: Lena challenged the claim and asked where the numbers had come from.
words.ex2: The lawyer challenged the witness's story by pointing to a different time on the video.
words.nonExample: Nodding along with every statement without a question is not challenging it.

apps.academic: A reader can challenge a source by asking who wrote it and how the writer knows.
apps.spoken: I'd like to challenge that: where did you get the number?
apps.writing: Use challenge with a claim or an idea: challenge a claim, challenge a ruling.

cloze.s: Before accepting the statistic, Nia decided to ___ it and check the original source.

cloze2.s: A good debater will politely ___ a weak argument instead of letting it pass.

misuse.s: He challenged the claim by agreeing with every word and asking for nothing more.
misuse.why: To challenge is to question and ask for proof; agreeing with everything does neither.

visual.alt: A raised eyebrow beside a question mark.

words.frame: I would challenge the claim that ___ because ___.

words.def: To suggest a plan or idea for others to consider.
words.ex: Marcus proposed that the club meet on Thursdays instead of Mondays.
words.ex2: The mayor proposed a new bike lane along the river road.
words.nonExample: Keeping an idea to yourself is not proposing it.

apps.academic: In a meeting, a member may propose a motion before the group votes.
apps.spoken: I propose that we take a break.
apps.writing: Use propose before a plan, or before that and a new idea.

cloze.s: At the meeting, Aisha stood up to ___ a plan for a new recycling program.

cloze2.s: I ___ that we vote now, since everyone has had a chance to speak.

misuse.s: Eli proposed a plan by refusing to share it with anyone in the room.
misuse.why: To propose is to put an idea forward for others; keeping it hidden is the opposite.

visual.alt: A light bulb above a person speaking.

words.def: To state something firmly as true.
words.ex: Tomas asserted that the answer was twelve and then showed his work.
words.ex2: The defendant asserted his innocence in a calm, steady voice.
words.nonExample: Saying 'maybe' or 'I'm not sure' is not asserting.

apps.academic: A writer asserts a claim and then supports it with evidence.
apps.spoken: I assert that we can finish before dinner.
apps.writing: Use assert for a firm claim; follow it with a reason or proof.

cloze.s: In her essay, Jada will ___ that school uniforms should be optional and then give three reasons.

cloze2.s: The witness ___ that she had seen the car run the red light.

misuse.s: He asserted his claim by saying he was not sure and that it might be wrong.
misuse.why: To assert is to state firmly; saying you are unsure is not firm.

visual.alt: A raised finger beside a megaphone.

words.def: A general agreement reached by most or all of the people in a group.
words.ex: After an hour of talking, the committee reached a consensus on the date.
words.ex2: There is a strong scientific consensus that regular exercise improves health.
words.nonExample: A vote of six to five is not a consensus.

apps.academic: Scientists share a consensus when most experts agree after reviewing the evidence.
apps.spoken: We need to reach a consensus before the bell.
apps.writing: Use consensus with reach, build, or form; it already means agreement, so skip 'general consensus'.

cloze.s: The class reached a ___ about the field trip: every student agreed on the science museum.

cloze2.s: Instead of voting, the neighbors kept talking until they reached a ___ that everyone could accept.

misuse.s: The group reached a consensus even though half of them loudly disagreed with the plan.
misuse.why: A consensus is a general agreement; half the group disagreeing means there is none.

visual.alt: A group of people beside a check mark.

words.def: To agree with someone or share the same opinion.
words.ex: I concur with Priya that the plan needs a stronger ending.
words.ex2: Two doctors examined the patient, and both concurred that rest was needed.
words.nonExample: Arguing against an idea is not concurring with it.

apps.academic: In a debate, a speaker may concur with a point before adding a new reason.
apps.writing: Use concur with a person or point: concur with the committee.

cloze.s: When Sam said the park needed more benches, Lila nodded and said, "I ___ with that."

cloze2.s: The two judges ___ on the score, so the scoreboard showed the same number twice.

misuse.s: She concurred with the proposal by explaining why she strongly disagreed with it.
misuse.why: To concur is to agree; explaining strong disagreement is the opposite.

visual.alt: A thumbs-up beside a speech bubble.

words.def: To say something again, often to make it clear.
words.ex: The principal reiterated that no one may leave campus during lunch.
words.ex2: To reiterate, the project is due on Friday, not Monday.
words.nonExample: Saying a new idea for the first time is not reiterating.
words.rel: saying it again to be clear

apps.academic: A conclusion often reiterates the main claim in new words.
apps.spoken: Let me reiterate: please walk, don't run.
apps.writing: Use reiterate to restate a point in your conclusion, with fresh wording.

cloze.s: The coach had to ___ the rules before the game because several players had forgotten them.

cloze2.s: Let me ___ the main point: the field trip is canceled, not postponed.

misuse.s: He reiterated his point by introducing a brand-new idea he had never mentioned.
misuse.why: To reiterate is to say something again; a brand-new idea is not a repeat.

visual.alt: A circular arrow beside a person speaking.

words.def: To suddenly add a remark while someone else is speaking.
words.ex: Dani interjected a quick question while the guide was explaining the map.
words.ex2: "Excuse me," Mr. Cole interjected, "but the bell has already rung."
words.nonExample: Waiting until a speaker finishes and then raising a hand is not interjecting.

apps.academic: Debate rules say not to interject while the other team is speaking.
apps.spoken: Sorry to interject, but I have one quick question.
apps.writing: Use interject for a remark that breaks into someone else's turn to speak.

cloze.s: May I ___ for a second? I think the answer on the board has a typo.

cloze2.s: Her little brother kept trying to ___ jokes while she was giving her presentation.

misuse.s: He interjected by waiting silently until the speaker had finished.
misuse.why: To interject is to break in while someone is speaking; waiting silently is not breaking in.

visual.alt: A raised hand beside a speech bubble.

words.frame: It can be rude to interject when ___.

passage.title: The Reading Time Vote
paras: Ms. Reyes's sixth-grade class was deciding whether to add ten minutes of silent reading to the end of each day. Before the discussion began, she reminded everyone of the rules: respond to the person who spoke before you, and back up every claim with a reason.
Dev went first. "I propose that we add the reading time," he said. "I assert that it will help us. When my cousin's class tried it, their reading scores went up."
Lena raised her hand. "I want to acknowledge that Dev's idea has strong points," she said. "Quiet time sounds relaxing. But I challenge the claim about scores. One class is not enough proof."

"Sorry to interject," Omar said, "but we only have five minutes left, and I think we should hear from everyone." Ms. Reyes thanked him and asked Dev to reiterate his main point so that quieter students could follow. "To emphasize the key idea," Dev said, "ten minutes costs us nothing, and it gives everyone time with a book."

Priya spoke last. "I concur that the cost is small," she said. "Let's try it for two weeks and measure what happens." Several students nodded. After a few more comments, the class reached a consensus: they would try silent reading for two weeks and then vote again with real results.
Ms. Reyes smiled. "That went well because each of you listened and responded to what the last person said," she told them.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "interject" most nearly means
choices: to add a remark while someone else is talking
qs.why: Omar speaks up in the middle of the discussion to remind everyone about the time.

qs.q: Why does Lena challenge Dev's claim about scores?
choices: She wants to end the discussion.
She thinks that one class is not enough proof.
She believes Dev's cousin made up the story.
qs.why: Lena says one class is not enough proof, so she questions whether the claim is supported.

qs.q: Which detail best shows that Lena acknowledged Dev's idea before disagreeing?
choices: She said she wanted to acknowledge that Dev's idea had strong points.
She asked Ms. Reyes for more time.
qs.why: She names the strength in Dev's idea first and then raises her disagreement.

choices: a close vote of six to five
a general agreement that most or all can accept
qs.why: The class agreed on a trial of two weeks and a new vote, which most or all accepted.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: A discussion works best when speakers listen, respond, and use reasons.
Silent reading always improves test scores.
Teachers should end every discussion early.
The loudest speaker should decide for the class.
qs.why: Ms. Reyes ends by saying the discussion went well because each student listened and responded.

write.prompt: Write a short exchange between two or three students who are deciding something for their class. Use at least four words from this unit to show how they talk to each other.
write.frame: "I propose that ___," said ___. "I acknowledge ___, but I challenge ___," replied ___.

study.task: Choose two words from the unit that begin with re-, con-, or inter-. Explain how the prefix connects to the meaning, then write a sentence that shows how each word sounds in a real discussion.

shades.label: how firmly an idea is stated

sentences: Write a sentence in which a speaker acknowledges one strong point before challenging another.
Write a sentence that uses assert and a piece of evidence that supports the claim.
Write a sentence about a time when it was polite to interject and a time when it was not.
Write a sentence that uses propose and consensus to describe how a group makes a decision.

given: Lena agreed that Dev's idea had strong points.
She did not accept his claim.
combine.model: Lena acknowledged the strong points in Dev's idea, but she challenged his claim and asked for proof.
The coach reiterated the rules because the players had forgotten them before the game began.

discuss: What is the difference between concur and acknowledge? Give a sentence for each.
Is a consensus always the best way for a group to decide? Explain.
When is it helpful to reiterate a point, and when does it become repetitive?
produce.explain: Explain how assert and propose are different. Use a short example from a class discussion for each.

argue.prompt: Claim: Class decisions should be made by consensus, not by voting. Take a side and support it with two reasons, using words from this unit.
argue.frame: I believe that ___ because ___. A group that reaches a consensus can ___, but voting would ___.

constructed.prompt: A classmate claims that homework should be banned. Write a response that acknowledges one good point and challenges another.
look: names a real strength in the claim
asks for proof or gives a reason for disagreement
constructed.model: I acknowledge that homework can be stressful, but I challenge the idea that it should be banned. Practice at home helps me remember what I learned, so what evidence shows that students learn just as well without it?

constructed.prompt: Write a short exchange of three sentences in which one student proposes an idea, another concurs, and the group reaches a consensus.
look: shows a real idea being proposed
constructed.model: "I propose that we hold the bake sale on Friday," said Jun. "I concur, because more families pick up students then," said Rosa. After a short talk, the group reached a consensus on Friday.

constructed.prompt: A speaker is explaining safety rules when a student interjects. Write what happens next, using interject, reiterate, and emphasize.
look: shows the interruption and the speaker's response
uses emphasize to show what matters most
constructed.model: A student interjected with a question in the middle of the safety talk. The coach reiterated the rule about walking in the halls and emphasized that running could cause a serious fall.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten verbs and nouns that name the moves people make in a discussion. They use a short dialogue as a model, practice choosing the verb that fits a move, study the prefixes re-, con-, and inter-, and write their own exchanges and short arguments.

notes.va.respond.v: Respond means answer or react. Write the rule on the board: respond before you add. Practice with sentence stems. Students sometimes confuse respond with respect; both start with re-, but the meanings are different.
notes.va.acknowledge.v: Acknowledge means show you noticed or accept. Model acknowledging a point you disagree with. Students often think acknowledge means agree; it can come before disagreement.
notes.va.emphasize.v: Emphasize is to give importance. Show how voice, repetition, underlining, and placement each emphasize a point. Contrast with downplay.
notes.va.challenge.v: Teach the verb as questioning and asking for proof, not as a fight. Name the noun use (a difficult task) as a second sense. Role-play a polite challenge.
notes.va.propose.v: Propose is to put an idea forward. Contrast with assert: a proposal suggests a plan; an assertion states a claim. Students may know propose only as a marriage word; note it as a different use.
notes.va.assert.v: Assert is a firm claim. Use the shades ladder (suggest, propose, assert, insist). Link to assertive from grade 5. Ask what a good assertion needs next: evidence.
notes.va.consensus.n: Consensus is a general agreement, not a vote. Avoid the phrase general consensus, which is redundant. Ask students to consider how a group could build consensus without voting.
notes.va.concur.v: Concur means agree. Use in formal discussion and writing. Compare with acknowledge: you can acknowledge without concurring. Role-play two speakers who concur and two who differ.
notes.va.reiterate.v: Reiterate means say again, often for clarity. Contrast with repeat in a bored voice. Ask students to reiterate a main idea in new words as a conclusion move.
notes.va.interject.v: Interject means break in. Show the parts: inter- (between) plus ject (throw). Note that the noun interjection also names words like wow. Discuss when interjecting is rude and when it is helpful.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'Lena says she wants to acknowledge that Dev's idea has strong points, and then she says she challenges the claim about scores. So she does not agree and she does not ignore him. She names a good point first and then asks for proof. That is a useful move in a discussion.'
discuss: Which discussion verb do you need to practice most?
How does a speaker sound different when they assert and when they propose?
misconceptions: Challenge is the same as argue or fight.
extend: Record a short class discussion and label each turn with a verb from the unit.
Write a dialogue between two characters who reach a consensus after a disagreement.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the three groups (putting forward, reacting, agreeing) two days later with a role-play card sort, then at one week with a mini-discussion in which students must use at least four words. Connect to insist, persuasive, logical, and convince from earlier units.

frames: I acknowledge that ___, but I challenge ___.
I propose that we ___. I concur with ___ because ___.
To reiterate, ___. I want to emphasize that ___.
wida.oral: Partner A makes a claim about school. Partner B responds by acknowledging one point and challenging another, using words from the unit.

needsReview: Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: responder, reconocer (acknowledge and admit overlap), enfatizar, cuestionar (challenge), proponer, afirmar, consenso, estar de acuerdo (concur), reiterar, interrumpir con un comentario.

Sense boundaries: acknowledge combines 'accept as true' and 'show you noticed'; challenge taught as a verb with the noun sense in senses; propose does not teach the marriage sense; interject noun sense (interjection) is in a teacher note only.
Passage is a fictional classroom discussion; the claim that a cousin's class improved reading scores is a student's unverified statement within the story.
